opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, because it gets at the core tension in what we're building.

The way I think about it is that the deterministic digital stack we've inherited spends an enormous amount of energy fighting noise. Every transistor is biased far enough above the thermal floor that you can pretend the world is clean and Boolean. That's a beautiful abstraction, but it's very expensive. And a lot of the workloads we care about now, generative models, Bayesian inference, sampling from energy-based models, actually *want* randomness. So we end up burning energy to suppress noise, then burning more energy to synthesize pseudo-random numbers to put the noise back in. That's kind of absurd from a physics standpoint.

So the philosophy is: let physics do what physics does naturally, and use deterministic computation for what it's good at. The stochastic part of the chip is essentially an analog system whose dynamics follow something like Langevin dynamics. You have a set of continuous degrees of freedom coupled through programmable interactions, and you let them thermalize. The thermal fluctuations aren't a bug; they're the engine. When the system relaxes, it's sampling from a Boltzmann-like distribution defined by the energy landscape you've programmed in. That's exactly the primitive you need for probabilistic machine learning.

The deterministic side handles the parts where you need precision and control: setting the couplings and biases, reading out samples, accumulating statistics, computing gradients, and running the outer optimization loop. So it's a hybrid. Think of it as a digital controller orchestrating a physical sampler, rather than trying to make one paradigm do everything.

The hard engineering problems live at the interface. How do you get information in and out of the analog domain without the conversion costs eating your energy advantage? How do you calibrate against device mismatch and drift? How do you make the noise *the right kind* of noise, with the right temperature and correlation structure, so it actually corresponds to the distribution you think you're sampling? A lot of our work is figuring out how to co-design the algorithms with the hardware so they're robust to the imperfections of real physical systems, and in some cases exploit them.

Zooming out, I see this as part of a broader shift. For decades we've treated computation as an abstract mathematical thing that happens to be implemented in matter. I think the next era is going to treat computation as a physical process first, and ask: what's the most natural, energy-efficient way for matter to do the computation we want? For probabilistic AI, the answer looks a lot like thermodynamics.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that for a long time we've been fighting physics. Classical digital computing is this heroic effort to take a fundamentally noisy, stochastic, analog substrate and squash it into clean ones and zeros. You pump in energy, you build in error correction, you make the transistors big enough and the voltages high enough that thermal fluctuations are negligible. And that works great, it got us here. But it's wasteful, and it's especially wasteful for the kinds of workloads we actually care about now, which are probabilistic. Sampling, Bayesian inference, generative modeling, the whole diffusion paradigm. You're using a deterministic machine to painstakingly emulate randomness, which is a bit absurd when randomness is the free thing nature hands you.

So at Extropic the philosophy is, don't fight the noise, harness it. You build analog circuits where the thermal fluctuations of the electrons are the computational resource. You design the energy landscape of the circuit so that its equilibrium distribution, its Boltzmann distribution, is the distribution you want to sample from. Then you let physics relax, and the system literally does Langevin dynamics for you, at the speed and energy scale of the device itself, rather than you simulating Langevin dynamics with floating point ops.

Now, to your actual question, how do you marry that to deterministic computation, because you obviously can't just have a box of noise. A few things. First, the programming is deterministic. You set the parameters, the couplings and biases that shape the energy landscape, with precise digital control. That's your interface to the stochastic core. So you get a clean separation: the digital side decides what distribution you want, the thermodynamic side draws from it. Second, the readout is where it crosses back. You threshold or integrate the analog state and you get samples out as bits, so downstream it looks like any other data source to a conventional processor. Third, and this is the part people miss, you don't try to make the stochastic part do everything. You identify the subroutine in your algorithm that's fundamentally a sampling problem, the inner loop that's burning most of the compute, and you offload exactly that. Everything around it, the orchestration, the gradient bookkeeping, the stuff that genuinely wants to be exact, stays on the digital side.

The way I like to frame it is it's a hybrid architecture in the same spirit as GPU plus CPU, except the accelerator's native primitive isn't a matrix multiply, it's a draw from a probability distribution. And then there's a nice formal story underneath, because when you write down the dynamics it's all very clean in the language of stochastic differential equations and nonequilibrium thermodynamics. The deterministic part of the SDE is the drift, which you program, and the stochastic part is the diffusion, which the physics provides. So the combination isn't a hack, it's literally what the equation is telling you to do.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that you don’t want to eliminate stochasticity everywhere. You want to use it where it’s computationally useful and bring in deterministic control where you need precision and orchestration.

In a thermodynamic system, you can encode a problem into an energy landscape and let the physical dynamics explore that landscape. Thermal fluctuations become a resource for sampling, rather than simply noise that you have to suppress. But that doesn’t mean you just let the system fluctuate and expect the right answer. You have to engineer the interactions, control the dynamics, and understand the distribution you’re actually sampling from.

So the architecture is naturally hybrid. Deterministic computation handles things like setting up the problem, programming parameters, and processing the results. The stochastic physical component does the sampling. The central engineering question is whether that physical evolution can deliver useful samples more efficiently than simulating the same process digitally, once you account for control, readout, and communication costs.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is to make the stochastic physics part of the computation, rather than something you’re constantly trying to suppress. In conventional computing, you spend energy making devices behave deterministically. For probabilistic computation, those fluctuations can actually be useful: you want to generate samples from a distribution.

So you design a physical system whose dynamics correspond to the probabilistic model you want to run. You control its couplings and biases, and let it fluctuate and explore possible configurations. The challenge is making sure those physical dynamics produce the distribution you intended, on a useful timescale.

The deterministic computer still has an essential role. It sets up the problem, controls the parameters, reads out samples, and handles the parts of the algorithm that require precise arithmetic. You can think of it as a digital controller working with a thermodynamic sampling engine.

The goal isn’t to replace every deterministic operation with noise. It’s to identify where an algorithm needs randomness, and ask whether the physics can do that work more efficiently than a digital simulation of the same process.
